name: Decoden / keitai rhinestone art

card.summary: A Japanese craft of covering phones, cases and nails with rhinestones, charms and resin, associated with gyaru style and used to complete a decorated, glam look.
card.note: Nail charms and glue can snag or lift natural nails; adhesive allergies are possible.

quick.overview:
Decoden, also called keitai deco, is a craft from Japan in which phones and other devices are decorated with acrylic, rhinestones, crystals, silicone and polymer clay. It is associated with gyaru fashion.

For looks, the same bling shows up on long artificial nails with 3D charms and as part of the gyaru styling that also includes dramatic makeup and voluminous hair.
quick.how: Decorations were once glued directly onto phones and are now usually applied to smartphone cases. Gyaru nail sets use the same rhinestones and charms.
quick.risks: Little documented. Long decorated nails can catch or break, and adhesives can irritate some people.

lead: Decoden, also called keitai art, is a gyaru-associated hobby that originated in Japan. It involves decorating phones and devices with acrylic, rhinestones, crystals, silicone and polymer clay.[1]

Older decorations were glued directly onto phones, while newer ones are usually applied to smartphone cases.[1] Gyaru nails are typically long, artificial and heavily decorated, with 3D charms among the elements, so the style carries over to personal grooming.[1]
Gyaru itself is known for tanned skin, voluminous dyed hair, dramatic eye makeup and large lashes.[1] No studies have examined decoden.

chain: Rhinestones and charms applied to nails and accessories
angle.text: Rhinestone and charm decoration on nails and accessories adds the glam finish of the gyaru look.

infobox: Acrylic, rhinestones, crystals, silicone, polymer clay[1]

paras: Decoden covers items with decorative pieces; keitai refers to Japanese mobile phones. The practice is paired with collecting phone charms and taking purikura photo-sticker pictures.[1]
In 2009 Acer held a decoden contest for its Aspire One netbook.[1]

timeline.event: Acer runs a decoden contest for the Aspire One.[1]
